ਮੇਰਾ ਗੁਰੁ ਪਰਮੇਸਰੁ ਸੁਖਦਾਈ ॥:
The speaker declares that their Guru is the Transcendent Lord himself, the one who bestows all peace and comfort. This identification means the spiritual teacher is not merely a guide but God in form, the source from which all solace and wellbeing flow. The possessive "my" expresses intimate belonging and devoted relationship with the one who grants tranquility to the seeker.

Themes: Guru as Divine, peace-giver, Transcendent Lord, spiritual teacher, devotion, identity of Guru and God, source of comfort, personal relationship with the Divine
ਤੁਮ ਦਾਤੇ ਤੁਮ ਪੁਰਖ ਬਿਧਾਤੇ ॥:
The Divine is declared the sole giver of all gifts and the Creator who brings beings into existence. God is both the benefactor who provides for creatures and the all-pervading Presence who sustains creation. These roles—giver, creator, sustainer—belong to the One alone. This is praise through recognition, acknowledging complete dependence on divine providence and establishing the proper relationship between creature and Creator.

Themes: divine attributes, God as creator, God as giver, omnipresence, providence, sovereignty, dependence on God, praise
ਕਰੁਣਾ ਮੈ ਕਿਰਪਾਲ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਨਿਧਿ ਜੀਵਨ ਪਦ ਨਾਨਕ:
The seeker addresses the Divine as the embodied source of compassion, the merciful one, the treasure-house of grace, invoking these qualities as both praise and the basis for appeal. The sacred vision (darshan) of the Divine is named as that which grants the elevated spiritual status, the true life worth living. The teeka reads this as a plea for that vision, while the translation states it as received; either way, divine mercy is the cause and divine presence the gift that transforms existence into its proper purpose.

Themes: divine mercy, darshan (sacred vision), jivan pad (state of true life), compassion, grace, spiritual elevation, devotional address, refuge in divine presence.
ਤੂੰ ਭਾਰੋ ਠਾਕੁਰੁ ਗੁਣੀ ਗਹੇਰਾ ॥੨॥:
Declares the Divine as the supreme sovereign Lord, an inexhaustible reservoir of virtues whose depth cannot be fathomed. Praises God as both the accessible treasure of excellence and the profoundly deep, unfathomable reality beyond human measure. Affirms divine mastery while acknowledging that divine qualities are simultaneously abundant and immeasurably profound, evoking reverent submission to a master whose nature exceeds full comprehension.

Themes: divine sovereignty, unfathomable depth, virtue and excellence, praise and adoration, God as master, immeasurable qualities, reverent submission
ਦੇਵਣਹਾਰੁ ਦਾਤਾਰੁ ਕਿਤੁ ਮੁਖਿ ਸਾਲਾਹੀਐ ॥:
The Divine is the great Giver, the generous Provider who sustains all beings, and no mouth can adequately praise Him. The rhetorical question exposes the vast gap between God's boundless generosity and the creature's limited capacity for gratitude. Human speech cannot match divine giving; the tongue falls short before the One who bestows all sustenance. This is humble acknowledgment that giving belongs entirely to God while praising remains forever incomplete.

Themes: divine generosity, human inadequacy, limits of praise, humility, God as Provider, gratitude, sustenance, devotional wonder
ਤੇਰੇ ਕਵਨ ਕਵਨ ਗੁਣ ਕਹਿ ਕਹਿ ਗਾਵਾ ਤੂ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਗ:
The speaker asks a rhetorical question expressing devotional overwhelm: which of the Divine's countless virtues should be sung when they exceed all counting? The question itself becomes praise, acknowledging the Lord as the boundless treasure-house of all excellence, the master and sustainer of all. Human speech cannot compass divine infinitude; the devotee can only marvel at such inexhaustible fullness.

Themes: divine virtues, devotional overwhelm, treasure of qualities, rhetorical praise, infinite nature of the Divine, Lord as sustainer, impossibility of complete description, wonder
ਰੇ ਬਉਰੇ ਤੁਹਿ ਘਰੀ ਨ ਰਾਖੈ ਕੋਈ ॥:
The speaker addresses the deluded mind as mad and warns that when the time comes, no one will offer shelter even for a moment. This is an admonishment about the consequences of spiritual blindness: worldly attachments and relationships prove temporary, and those lost in maya (worldly illusion) will find themselves utterly abandoned. The warning exposes that misplaced trust in transient things leaves one with no refuge when it matters most.

Themes: impermanence of worldly shelter, consequences of spiritual delusion, abandonment at the final hour, warning to the foolish mind, futility of maya, transience, refuge denied, wake-up call.
ਕਾਹੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਡੋਲਤਾ ਹਰਿ ਮਨਸਾ ਪੂਰਣਹਾਰੁ ॥:
The mind is directly questioned for its instability and wavering, challenged to recognize that the Divine fulfills all hopes and desires. The speaker admonishes their own consciousness for unnecessary anxiety, pointing to God as the one who satisfies every longing and need. This is counsel to the self, urging the restless mind toward steadiness by remembering that the Lord is the accomplisher of wishes and the answer to all wants.

Themes: mind's instability, divine fulfiller of desires, self-admonition, trust over anxiety, God as satisfier of needs, counsel to one's own consciousness, remembrance of divine providence, steadying the wavering mind.
ਰੇ ਮਨ ਤੂ ਭੀ ਭਜੁ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ॥੨॥:
The speaker directly addresses their own mind with urgent instruction, commanding it to remember and seek refuge in Gobind, the Lord who tends the universe. The phrase "you too" implies others have already turned toward the Divine, and the mind must not remain behind in its wandering. This is an admonition, a call to action urging the consciousness toward bhajan—loving remembrance and meditation on the divine Name that anchors the soul.

Themes: self-admonition, addressing the mind, meditation, bhajan, divine remembrance, Gobind, spiritual urgency, refuge
ਮਨ ਮੇਰਿਆ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਤੇਰੈ ਨਿਧਾਨੁ ਹੈ ਬਾਹਰਿ ਵਸਤੁ:
The speaker addresses their own mind, declaring that the true treasure—the Divine presence, source of all comfort—already dwells within the heart. The mind is instructed to stop searching for this precious substance in external places like forests or wilderness. The line corrects the misdirected impulse to seek God outwardly when the Lord resides in the innermost self. The treasure is both an image of hidden wealth and the reality of the Divine presence within.

Themes: inner divine presence, self-instruction, futility of external seeking, treasure within, admonition to mind, antar (inner) vs bahir (outer), spiritual wealth, God as nidhan
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਤੂ ਕਾਏ ਦੇਖਿ ਭੁਲਾਨਾ ॥:
The line directly addresses the mind as a fool infatuated with maya (worldly attachment), demanding it listen and questioning why it goes astray after seeing worldly illusion. The rebuke exposes the mind's error: gazing at maya's attractions causes it to lose its way from the true purpose of human life. The speaker admonishes their own consciousness, diagnosing spiritual delusion and urging awakening from attachment-induced confusion.

Themes: maya and worldly attachment, admonishing the mind, spiritual delusion, going astray from life's purpose, wake-up call, self-correction, infatuation with illusion, listening to wisdom
ਸੁਣਿ ਬਾਵਰੇ ਥੀਉ ਰੇਣੁ ਜਿਨੀ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਧਿਆਇਆ ॥:
The line addresses the spiritually deluded as "madman" and commands radical humility: becoming dust beneath the feet of those who practice simran (loving remembrance) of the Divine. The dust image conveys complete self-effacement and surrender, positioning the seeker at the lowest place in relation to the devout—the very path to union with God. The instruction prescribes sangat (company of the devoted) as essential, accessed through utter humility rather than intellectual effort.

Themes: humility, sangat (company of the devoted), simran (loving remembrance), self-surrender, spiritual delusion, divine union, service to the holy, ego dissolution
ਲਖ ਖੁਸੀਆ ਪਾਤਿਸਾਹੀਆ ਜੇ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਨਦਰਿ ਕਰੇਇ:
The line declares that a single merciful glance from the True Guru brings joy equivalent to hundreds of thousands of royal pleasures and kingly delights. It establishes divine grace as the supreme source of happiness, surpassing all worldly wealth, status, and material enjoyment. The devotee who receives the Guru's compassionate attention experiences total fulfillment, as if every worldly treasure has been obtained.

Themes: divine grace, Guru's glance, true happiness, worldly pleasures versus spiritual joy, contentment, mercy, spiritual wealth, fulfillment
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਹੋਇ ਦਇਆਲੁ ਤਾ ਦੁਖੁ ਨ ਜਾਣੀਐ ॥:
The line declares that the Satguru's mercy fundamentally alters how suffering is experienced. When the True Guru shows compassion, the devotee no longer recognizes pain as pain—hardship may still arrive, but it is not felt as affliction. This is not the absence of difficulty but a transformed relationship to it, where divine grace so saturates awareness that worldly distress loses its sting.

Themes: Satguru's mercy, transformed perception, end of suffering, divine grace, liberation from pain, spiritual refuge, changed consciousness, relief from affliction
ਹਰਿ ਚਉਥੜੀ ਲਾਵ ਮਨਿ ਸਹਜੁ ਭਇਆ ਹਰਿ ਪਾਇਆ ਬਲਿ:
The fourth marriage round marks the soul's complete union with the Divine, where the mind attains sahaj—its natural state of spiritual equipoise and steadfast stability. The wedding imagery of the lav ceremony symbolizes the culmination of spiritual seeking: the soul-bride finds the Divine Bridegroom and restless searching ends in peaceful fulfillment. This declares the fruit of devotion—inner peace and divine presence realized through the journey of four stages.

Themes: spiritual union, sahaj, fourth lav, divine attainment, soul-bride, inner peace, completion, wedding symbolism
ਸੁਖੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮਨਾਇ ॥:
Satisfying the True Guru (satguru) by enshrining the Guru within the heart yields peace and all desired fruits. The declaration states a direct causal relationship: inner contentment and complete fulfillment come from aligning with the Guru's will and internalizing the Guru's presence. Personal testimony of having found peace doubles as implicit instruction—pleasing the Guru is the means to obtain every sought outcome.

Themes: satguru, inner peace, heart-enshrinement, fulfillment, surrender to Guru's will, divine contentment, Guru-pleasing, desired fruits
ਸਤਿਗੁਰੁ ਮੇਰਾ ਸਦਾ ਸਹਾਈ ਜਿਨਿ ਦੁਖ ਕਾ ਕਾਟਿਆ:
The speaker declares that the True Guru provides eternal support, having torn down the banner of suffering that marks pain's dominion over human life. The image of cutting the root of distress signifies not temporary relief but permanent removal of misery from its source. This is a statement of complete trust in the Guru as the one who eliminates suffering at its origin and remains a constant helper for those who take refuge.

Themes: True Guru, eternal support, end of suffering, refuge, removal of pain's root, trust, liberation from distress, divine protection
ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਮਿਲਣ ਕੀ ਇਹ ਤੇਰੀ ਬਰੀਆ ॥:
This present moment is declared the sole opportunity for union with Gobind, the Lord of the Universe. The direct address creates urgency around spiritual seeking, emphasizing that such a chance is rare and must not be wasted. Human birth itself is the precious occasion for divine meeting, the opening through which the soul can merge with its source.

Themes: divine union, urgency of spiritual practice, human birth as opportunity, Gobind, rare chance, soul's meeting with God, spiritual awakening, seizing the moment
ਪ੍ਰਾਣੀ ਤੂੰ ਆਇਆ ਲਾਹਾ ਲੈਣਿ ॥:
The mortal is addressed directly and reminded that human birth was granted for one purpose: to accumulate spiritual wealth through naam (the divine Name). The commercial metaphor of earning profit frames life as a brief trading opportunity where the soul must gather what endures beyond death. Worldly gains are false profit; the only true earning is devotion and remembrance of the Divine. This is an urgent call to recognize why one has come into this world and not squander the chance.

Themes: purpose of human life, naam as spiritual profit, merchant metaphor, true wealth versus material gain, opportunity of human birth, divine remembrance, awakening the mortal, simran (loving remembrance).
ਹਰਿ ਭਗਤਿ ਦ੍ਰਿੜੁ ਮਿਲੁ ਸਾਧ ਨਾਨਕ ਤੇਰੈ ਕਾਮਿ:
The speaker addresses the self, instructing it to meet the Guru and firmly root devotion to the Divine within the heart. Holy association makes loving worship steadfast and unshakeable. This alone will serve one's true purpose and be of real use; nothing else ultimately matters. The declaration affirms that spiritual anchoring through the Guru's company is the sole meaningful pursuit in human life.

Themes: devotion, Guru's company, firm establishment, true purpose, self-instruction, spiritual utility, holy association, inner anchoring
ਜੀਵਨਾ ਸਫਲ ਜੀਵਨ ਸੁਨਿ ਹਰਿ ਜਪਿ ਜਪਿ ਸਦ ਜੀਵਨਾ:
Human life becomes fruitful and successful only through hearing the divine Name and then continually chanting and remembering it. The one who engages in this practice of listening to and repeating God's name lives eternally—their life attains lasting significance rather than passing without purpose. The line declares the criterion for a worthwhile human existence, establishing that the path to eternal life lies through auditory reception of sacred knowledge followed by constant vocal remembrance, praising the devotee who has made their life meaningful through this discipline.

Themes: purpose of human life, hearing sacred teaching, constant remembrance, eternal life, naam simran (loving remembrance of the divine Name), successful living, spiritual fulfillment, divine Name.
ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਆਧਾਰੁ ਜਨ ਕਾ ਆਸਰਾ ॥:
The Divine's lotus feet are proclaimed the sole foundation and refuge for devotees, the support that sustains life itself. The lotus feet represent both the beautiful presence of the Divine and the sacred point of surrender where the faithful find their true shelter and stability. Complete reliance on divine grace, rather than worldly anchors, defines the devotee's existence.

Themes: lotus feet, divine refuge, surrender, dependence on God, shelter for devotees, foundation of life, divine support, grace
ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਸੇਵੀ ਰਿਦ ਅੰਤਰਿ ਗੁਰ ਪੂਰੇ ਕੈ ਆਧਾਰਿ:
The devotee seeks mercy and takes refuge in the Perfect Guru, keeping meditation on the beautiful lotus feet firmly established within the heart. The lotus feet symbolize both the Divine presence and the state of complete surrender and spiritual shelter. Inner contemplation of the Divine becomes possible through reliance on the Guru's guidance. This is a personal declaration of devotional practice sustained by the Guru's support.

Themes: charan kamal (lotus feet), Guru's refuge, inner meditation, heart-centered devotion, surrender, spiritual support, simran, divine shelter.
ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਸਿਉ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਿ ਰੀਤਿ ਸੰਤਨ ਮਨਿ ਆਵਏ ਜੀਉ:
The line declares that loving attachment to the Divine's lotus feet is the defining way of life that dwells in the minds of the sant (devotees). The lotus feet symbolize both the presence of the Divine and the posture of surrender and refuge; preet (loving devotion) toward them is the reet (established tradition) that fills the inner landscape of the devout. This is a settled disposition, a discipline of the heart that marks the true seeker.

Themes: lotus feet, loving devotion, saints, mind, discipline, surrender, refuge, divine presence
ਬੋਹਿਥੜਾ ਹਰਿ ਚਰਣ ਮਨ ਚੜਿ ਲੰਘੀਐ ॥:
The Lord's feet are a vessel, a boat that ferries the soul across the world-ocean of suffering and rebirth. The speaker instructs their own mind to climb aboard, to take shelter at the divine feet, and thereby cross over to liberation. The ship image conveys protection from drowning in maya (worldly attachment) and transport toward the far shore. Surrender at the feet is the means of crossing; the destination is freedom from the cycle of existence.

Themes: divine feet as refuge, crossing the world-ocean, surrender and liberation, boat as spiritual vessel, instruction to the mind, taking shelter, liberation from rebirth
ਹਰਿ ਚਰਨ ਕਮਲ ਮਨੁ ਬੇਧਿਆ ਕਿਛੁ ਆਨ ਨ ਮੀਠਾ ਰਾਮ:
The mind pierced by the Lord's lotus feet finds no other sweetness anywhere; the Divine presence alone remains delightful once consciousness is transfixed and absorbed. This declares a state of exclusive devotion where the tender feet of the Divine become the single object of love, rendering all worldly attractions tasteless by comparison. The piercing is both wound and cure, an absorption that makes the devotee indifferent to all else.

Themes: lotus feet, exclusive devotion, absorption, sweetness of the Divine, pierced mind, single-pointed love, detachment from world, divine refuge
ਪੀ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਆਘਾਨਿਆ ਗੁਰਿ ਅਮਰੁ ਕਰਾਇਆ ॥੨॥:
The devotee drinks amrit, the ambrosial nectar of naam, and attains complete fulfillment; through the Guru's agency, he is made amar—immortal in a spiritual sense, meaning his inner state never decays, death cannot touch him, and suffering no longer reaches him. This declares the final result of absorbing divine essence: the soul grounded in the Guru attains deathlessness and permanent peace.

Themes: amrit, immortality, Guru's grace, spiritual fulfillment, liberation from death, freedom from suffering, divine nectar, naam
ਜਿਨ੍ਹ ਪੀਆ ਸੇ ਮਸਤ ਭਏ ਹੈ ਤੂਟੇ ਬੰਧਨ ਫਾਹੇ ॥:
Those who drink the essence of naam (the divine Name) become spiritually intoxicated, entering a state of divine ecstasy beyond ordinary awareness. The bonds and nooses of maya (worldly attachment) that entrap the soul are severed and fall away completely. This declares that absorption in the divine Name produces both an inner condition of enrapturement and the outer freedom of liberation from worldly entanglements.

Themes: naam, spiritual intoxication, liberation from maya, breaking bonds, divine absorption, freedom from attachment, transformation, naam-ras
ਹਰਿ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਸੋ ਚਖੈ ਮੇਰੇ ਮਨਾ ॥੨॥:
Addresses the mind directly, urging it to drink the ambrosial nectar of the divine Name — the Hari-naam that grants spiritual life. Those who partake of this immortal essence receive inner sustenance and awakening. The mind is being instructed to seek this life-giving elixir, the loving remembrance that nourishes the soul and confers eternal vitality.

Themes: amrit (ambrosial nectar), naam (divine Name), spiritual nourishment, mind's awakening, inner elixir, simran (loving remembrance), soul's sustenance, admonishing the mind
ਹਰਿ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਵਹੁ ਭਾਈ ॥:
The line exhorts spiritual siblings to drink the divine essence, using the image of consuming nectar to describe internalizing God's presence through naam (divine Name) practice. The teeka specifies this means taking refuge in the perfect Guru and continually remembering the divine Name. The metaphor of drinking suggests complete absorption and the deep satisfaction that comes from loving devotion rather than chasing worldly pleasures.

Themes: naam simran, divine nectar, Guru's refuge, spiritual instruction, loving remembrance, fellowship, absorption in God, satisfaction through devotion
ਗੁਰਿ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਹਰਿ ਮੁਖਿ ਚੋਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਜਿੰਦੁੜੀ:
The speaker addresses their own soul in gratitude, declaring that the Guru has poured amrit (immortal nectar of the divine Name) directly into their mouth, reviving them from spiritual death. The image of pouring into the mouth conveys unearned reception of grace, while the contrast between dying and being brought back to life captures the complete transformation that naam (divine Name) accomplishes. The soul, once perishing in spiritual death, receives new life through the Guru's intervention alone.

Themes: spiritual death and resurrection, Guru as life-giver, amrit as divine nectar, naam received through grace, transformation from spiritual death to life, revival of the soul, direct transmission, unmerited divine favor.
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਨਿਧਾਨੁ ਹੈ ਮਿਲਿ ਪੀਵਹੁ ਭਾਈ ॥:
The divine Name functions as immortalizing nectar and a hidden treasure, accessible only through gathering in sangat (company of the devout). The speaker urges fellow seekers to meet together and drink this spiritual essence, emphasizing that the Name must be internalized communally rather than pursued alone. This amrit sustains the soul and is found through shared devotion, not solitary effort.

Themes: amrit, naam, sangat, spiritual treasure, collective devotion, internalization, communal practice, siblinghood
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭਉ ਕਟਿਓਨੁ ਫਿਰਿ ਜੋਨਿ ਨ ਪਾਏ ॥:
The Divine eliminates the terror of repeated births and deaths, freeing the devotee from the cycle of transmigration. This liberation means never again entering the womb or returning to worldly existence. The statement declares the finality of mukti (liberation) as a gift of grace, where the soul escapes samsara (the cycle of reincarnation) entirely and the existential dread of dying and being reborn ceases.

Themes: liberation from rebirth, freedom from existential fear, divine grace ending transmigration, mukti, samsara, escape from cycle of birth and death, final release, soul's deliverance
ਸਹਜੁ ਭਇਆ ਪ੍ਰਭੁ ਪਾਇਆ ਜਮ ਕਾ ਭਉ ਲਥਾ ॥੨੦॥:
The line declares that when the mind attains sahaj (natural equipoise and inner stability), the Divine is found, and the fear of Yama, the messenger of death, is completely shed. This establishes a causal sequence: inner stillness leads to divine encounter, which dissolves existential terror. The teeka notes that spiritual death cannot approach one grounded in this poise.

Themes: sahaj (spiritual equipoise), divine encounter, liberation from fear of death, Yama, inner stability, freedom from existential dread, spiritual attainment, realized state
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭਉ ਕਟੀਐ ਜਨ ਕਾ ਸਬਦੁ ਜਪਿ ॥:
Declares that the terror of birth and death is severed by meditating on the shabad, the divine Word. The teeka specifies this happens within sangat (the company of the devout) through reciting hymns of praise, and reads "birth and death" as the fear pervading one's entire mortal span, not merely its endpoints. The instruction is prescriptive: repeat the sacred utterance and the dread of transmigration dissolves. Liberation from the cycle of coming and going is achieved through sustained remembrance of the divine Name in holy association.

Themes: birth-death cycle, fear of mortality, shabad meditation, sangat, liberation from transmigration, divine Word, recitation of praise, existential dread
ਨ ਦਨੋਤਿ ਜਸਮਰਣੇਨ ਜਨਮ ਜਰਾਧਿ ਮਰਣ ਭਇਅੰ ॥੧॥ ਰ:
Through simran (loving remembrance) of the Divine, the fear and suffering tied to birth, old age, anxiety, and death cease to torment. The teeka widens the scope beyond mortality to include worry and mental anguish as afflictions dissolved by holding the divine Name in consciousness. This refrain declares that meditative remembrance is the sole refuge from existential dread, promising that one who remembers the Eternal becomes free from the terrors of the embodied cycle.

Themes: simran, fear of death, liberation from suffering, birth and rebirth, anxiety, divine remembrance, mortality, refuge
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਦੁਖੁ ਕਾਟੀਐ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਚੂਕੈ ਜਮ ਕੀ ਕਾਣੇ:
Declares that the agony of repeated births and deaths is severed and the dread of the divine punisher, the messenger of death, fully extinguished. The teeka specifies this liberation occurs specifically within sangat (the company of the devout). Affirms that human suffering across the cycle of transmigration ends through association with devoted seekers, releasing one from the fear and authority of death's enforcer. The pain of coming and going is cut away; the terror of the soul-reaper collapses.

Themes: liberation from birth-death cycle, end of fear of death, sangat as means of release, severing transmigratory suffering, freedom from jam's authority, eradication of existential pain, company of the devout, overcoming mortality's dread
ਜਨਮ ਮਰਣ ਭੈ ਲਾਥੇ ॥੪॥੨॥੫੨॥:
The terror of endless rebirth and dying has been lifted. This declaration describes a state of spiritual freedom where the fundamental anxiety binding the soul to worldly existence has dissolved. The cycle of transmigration no longer generates dread because permanent refuge in the Divine has been found. Liberation from existential fear is attained through union with the eternal.

Themes: liberation from rebirth, freedom from existential fear, cycle of transmigration, spiritual attainment, divine refuge, removal of anxiety, birth and death, state of fearlessness
ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ ਕੈ ਆਸਰੈ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਸਿਉ ਰੰਗੁ ਲਾਏ ॥:
Taking refuge in sangat (the company of the devout) enables the heart to become colored with love for the Divine. The statement declares a causal relationship: holy fellowship is the support through which divine attachment develops. The seeker who relies on the company of devotees finds their affections transformed toward God. Love for the Divine arises not in isolation but through the influence of those already devoted.

Themes: sangat, divine love, refuge, fellowship, transformation of heart, devotion, spiritual community, attachment to God
ਸਾਧੂ ਸੰਗਿ ਤਰੀਜੈ ਸਾਗਰੁ ਕਟੀਐ ਜਮ ਕੀ ਫਾਸਾ ਜੀ:
Through sangat (the company of the devout), the seeker crosses the world-ocean—the vast expanse of worldly existence and maya (worldly attachment)—and severs the noose of death that binds the soul to cycles of rebirth. The line instructs that spiritual fellowship is the means of transcending samsara and escaping Yama's snare, the grip of mortality and karmic bondage. Both images—ocean-crossing and noose-cutting—convey liberation from the peril of embodied existence.

Themes: sangat, liberation, world-ocean, noose of death, samsara, Yama, spiritual fellowship, freedom from rebirth
ਸਾਧਸੰਗਤਿ ਕੀ ਭੀਰ ਜਉ ਪਾਈ ਤਉ ਨਾਨਕ ਹਰਿ ਸੰਗਿ:
The speaker declares that obtaining entry into the sadh sangat, the company of the devout, resulted in meeting the Lord. The gathering of holy fellowship is presented as the direct cause and condition for divine union. This testimony affirms that finding spiritual community leads to finding God. The bheer, the press or assembly of the holy, becomes the threshold where separation ends and union with the Divine begins.

Themes: sangat, divine union, spiritual fellowship, meeting the Lord, sadh sangat, community as path to God, grace, transformation through association
ਸੰਤਤ ਹੀ ਸਤਸੰਗਤਿ ਸੰਗ ਸੁਰੰਗ ਰਤੇ ਜਸੁ ਗਾਵਤ ਹ:
The saints perpetually dwell in sangat (the company of the devout), deeply dyed in divine love, and sing the Lord's praises. This declares the natural sequence of spiritual life: holy fellowship produces complete absorption in sacred love, which overflows as kirtan (devotional singing). The dyeing image conveys thorough saturation—the devotee becomes permeated with divine color through sustained association with the holy, not merely surface contact.

Themes: sangat, divine love, kirtan, spiritual absorption, saints, transformation, devotion, praise
ਕਾਢਿ ਲੀਏ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਆਨ ਬਿਖੈ ਤੇ ਸਾਧਸੰਗਿ ਮਨੁ ਲਾਵ:
The devotee pleads with the Divine to extract them from vices and worldly corruptions, and to attach their mind to the sangat, the company of the holy. This prayer of complete dependence acknowledges that both rescue from attachment and joining to holy fellowship are works of Divine grace the seeker cannot accomplish alone. The request names the two movements of spiritual life: being pulled from false attachments and being joined to true companionship.

Themes: prayer, supplication, liberation from vice, sangat (holy company), divine grace, attachment, mind, refuge
ਮਹਿਮਾ ਸਾਧੂ ਸੰਗ ਕੀ ਸੁਨਹੁ ਮੇਰੇ ਮੀਤਾ ॥:
The speaker addresses companions as friends, urging them to hear with attention the magnitude and excellence of the Guru's sangat (the company of the devout). This is an exhortation and invitation, calling listeners to attend to a truth worth knowing: that gathering with holy persons carries profound spiritual benefit and transformative power. The glory being declared is not abstract praise but an assertion that this company is the path to liberation.

Themes: sangat, holy company, spiritual fellowship, listening, invitation, exhortation, Guru's congregation, transformative gathering
ਸੰਤ ਜਨਾ ਕੀ ਰੇਣੁਕਾ ਲੈ ਮਾਥੈ ਲਾਵਉ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ:
The devotee prays to receive the dust from the feet of the saints and press it to the forehead, declaring this the supreme attainment. The teeka clarifies that this sacred dust equals the nine treasures of worldly wealth and the eighteen spiritual powers — meaning the humble residue of the holy surpasses all material riches and mystical accomplishments. Applying foot-dust to the brow is both a concrete gesture of self-abasement and a declaration that the lowest service to the devout is the highest honor. The seeker asks for nothing but this consecrated dust, treating contact with the holy as the ultimate blessing and sole currency worth earning.

Themes: dust of saints' feet, humility and surrender, forehead as mark of devotion, nine treasures, eighteen spiritual powers, reverence for the holy, divine gift, self-abasement
ਗੁਰਸਿਖਾਂ ਕੀ ਹਰਿ ਧੂੜਿ ਦੇਹਿ ਹਮ ਪਾਪੀ ਭੀ ਗਤਿ:
The speaker pleads with the Divine to grant them the dust from the feet of Guru's Sikhs, expressing profound humility by acknowledging their own sinful nature while seeking spiritual liberation through contact with the holy. The dust of feet is both a concrete image of prostration before the devout and a metaphorical statement that redemption comes through association with those walking the path of truth. Even the fallen can attain a high spiritual state through the blessing of sangat.

Themes: humility, prayer, sangat (company of the devout), spiritual aspiration, redemption of sinners, dust of feet, divine grace, surrender
ਕਰਉ ਨਮਸਕਾਰ ਭਗਤ ਜਨ ਧੂਰਿ ਮੁਖਿ ਲਾਵਉ ॥੩॥:
The speaker bows before bhagats (devotees) and applies the dust of their feet to the face—an act of supreme humility honoring the devotee as the source of spiritual merit. The teeka frames this as a prayer to join the sangat (company of the devout) for bhagti (devotional worship), so that through their association the speaker may also sing divine praises. The foot-dust marks the devotee's presence as sacred ground; applying it is both ritual honor and surrender, recognizing that progress flows through service to those who remember the divine Name.

Themes: humility, sangat, bhagti, surrender, devotees, foot-dust, reverence, divine association
ਟਹਲ ਕਰਉ ਤੇਰੇ ਦਾਸ ਕੀ ਪਗ ਝਾਰਉ ਬਾਲ ॥:
The speaker declares devotion through serving God's servant, wiping the devotee's feet with their own hair—an act of ultimate humility and reverence. This positions service to the bhagat (devotee) as the highest form of divine worship, recognizing that the path to the Divine runs through serving God's servants. The concrete image of hair at feet embodies both physical devotion and the spiritual principle that serving the sangat (company of the devout) is serving the Beloved.

Themes: seva (selfless service), humility, devotion to the devotee, sangat, surrender, feet as symbol of refuge, bhagat, serving the servant
ਕਰਿ ਕਿਰਪਾ ਧੂਰਿ ਦੇਹੁ ਸੰਤਨ ਕੀ ਸੁਖੁ ਨਾਨਕੁ ਇ:
The speaker petitions the Divine for grace, asking specifically to receive the dust from the feet of the holy ones, the sant jan. This dust is both a concrete image of taking the lowest position in humility and the spiritual refuge found in the company of the devout. The yearning expressed is for contact with the holy as the only true peace, the sole comfort sought. The devotee asks God directly for access to the sangat, the fellowship of the awakened.

Themes: divine grace, dust of saints' feet, humility, yearning for holy company, true peace, petition to God, sangat, spiritual refuge
ਸੰਤਹ ਚਰਣ ਹਮਾਰੋ ਮਾਥਾ ਨੈਨ ਦਰਸੁ ਤਨਿ ਧੂਰਿ ਪਰ:
The speaker prays for complete surrender at the feet of the holy ones, asking that their forehead remain bowed at the saints' feet, their eyes be blessed with the sacred vision (darshan) of the devout, and their body be covered with the dust from the saints' feet as a mark of blessing and total submission. This refrain line expresses intense longing for intimate connection with the company of the holy (sangat), positioning proximity to the devout as the highest good and the path to divine nearness. The imagery of feet, dust, and bowing conveys both physical humility and spiritual refuge, declaring that the speaker's entire being—head, eyes, body—seeks only the touch and sight of those who walk with the divine.

Themes: surrender, humility, longing for holy company, devotion to saints, darshan (sacred vision), refuge at holy feet, dust of the devout, prayer for spiritual connection
ਅਤਿ ਸੁੰਦਰ ਮਨਮੋਹਨ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਸਭਹੂ ਮਧਿ ਨਿਰਾਰੇ ॥:
The devotee addresses the Divine with intimate devotion, calling upon the supremely beautiful, mind-captivating Beloved who enthralls the heart. The central paradox declares that the Divine is simultaneously present within all creation yet fundamentally distinct from everything—immanent throughout existence while transcending all forms. The mystery unfolds of a God who pervades the world while remaining utterly unique, intimately accessible through love yet beyond full comprehension.

Themes: divine beauty, immanence and transcendence, divine paradox, beloved, mind-enthralling, devotion, divine presence, uniqueness of God
ਤੇਰਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਰੂੜੋ ਰੂਪੁ ਰੂੜੋ ਅਤਿ ਰੰਗ ਰੂੜੋ ਮੇ:
The devotee exclaims that the Divine Name, form, and love are each beautiful, repeating the adjective to build ecstatic praise. The Name (naam) is the sacred utterance through which God is known and invoked; the form is the manifest presence the devotee beholds; rang is both the image of divine color and the experience of being dyed in devotional love. The speaker claims the Lord intimately as their own, celebrating beauty that permeates every dimension of sacred encounter.

Themes: divine beauty, naam (the divine Name), rang (devotional absorption), intimate address, ecstatic praise, personal devotion, aesthetic spirituality, loving remembrance
ਸੁੰਦਰ ਰਸਾਲ ਤੂ ॥੧॥:
The speaker addresses the Divine directly, affirming two attributes: the Divine is beautiful beyond measure, and is the source of all rasa — the spiritual nectar, essence, and bliss that sustains the soul. This declaration of praise recognizes the Divine as the sole fountainhead of every sacred flavor, the wellspring from which all spiritual nourishment flows.

Themes: divine beauty, source of nectar, rasa, devotional praise, spiritual essence, fountainhead of bliss, direct address, sacred nourishment
ਨੈਣ ਪਸੰਦੋ ਸੋਇ ਪੇਖਿ ਮੁਸਤਾਕ ਭਈ ॥:
The soul declares that the Divine appears infinitely pleasing to her eyes, and upon beholding that presence, she becomes spiritually intoxicated, lost in ecstatic absorption. The image of eyes finding the Lord dear conveys both aesthetic attraction and the deep longing of the seeker for the Beloved. Seeing the Divine is not passive observation but a transformative encounter that produces masti—a state of rapture and self-forgetting joy in which the devotee is willingly captivated.

Themes: divine beauty, spiritual intoxication, longing for the Divine, vision of the Divine, ecstatic surrender, eyes as gateway to love, captivation by the Beloved, masti.
ਸੁੰਦਰ ਸੋਭਾ ਲਾਲ ਗੋਪਾਲ ਦਇਆਲ ਕੀ ਅਪਰ ਅਪਾਰਾ ਰ:
The line celebrates the beautiful, infinite glory of the Divine, who is the merciful sustainer of the world and the beloved of devotees. The splendor of this compassionate Lord spreads beyond all measure and limit. This is reverent praise naming the Divine as Gopal (sustainer of creation), Dayal (the Merciful One), and Laal (the Beloved), while affirming that His magnificence is boundless and immeasurable.

Themes: divine glory and splendor, infinite and boundless God, mercy and compassion, God as sustainer and protector, the Beloved Divine, praise and celebration, beauty of the Divine, devotion
ਅਪੁਨੇ ਸੇਵਕ ਕੀ ਆਪੇ ਰਾਖੈ ਆਪੇ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਾਵੈ ॥:
The Divine personally safeguards the honor and dignity of His devotees everywhere, and He Himself inspires their remembrance of the divine Name. This declares that the Lord does not merely accept devotion but actively generates it—protecting the servant while creating the very impulse toward simran (loving remembrance). The devotee does not earn protection or spiritual awakening through personal effort; both flow from the Divine's own initiative and grace.

Themes: divine protection, divine grace, naam simran, sevak (devotee), honor preservation, God as initiator, spiritual awakening, divine agency
ਭਗਤ ਜਨਾ ਕੀ ਹਰਿ ਜੀਉ ਰਾਖੈ ਜੁਗਿ ਜੁਗਿ ਰਖਦਾ ਆ:
The Divine Lord safeguards the honor of His bhagats (devotees), preserving their dignity and shielding them from disgrace. This protection spans all four yugs (cosmic ages)—establishing an eternal pattern of divine guardianship. The declaration affirms God's unwavering commitment to those who surrender in devotion, offering assurance that the faithful have always been upheld. The protection specifically concerns the devotee's honor and reputation rather than mere physical safety.

Themes: divine protection, bhagat (devotee), honor preservation, continuity across yugs, divine faithfulness, eternal guardianship, surrender, divine commitment
ਭਗਤ ਤੇਰੇ ਸਭਿ ਪ੍ਰਾਣਪਤਿ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਮ ਤੂੰ ਭਗਤਨ ਕਾ:
The line declares a reciprocal bond of love between the Divine and devotees: all devotees are dear to God, and God is beloved to them. Pranpati (Lord of life-breath) and Pritam (Beloved) name the Divine as both sustainer of existence and object of deepest affection. The relationship is mutual, not one-sided; the devotee's longing meets divine response. This affirmation offers comfort that sincere devotion is seen, valued, and returned.

Themes: reciprocal love, divine-devotee relationship, pranpati, pritam, mutual affection, bhagat, divine intimacy, devotion
ਭਗਤਾ ਕੀ ਟੇਕ ਤੂੰ ਸੰਤਾ ਕੀ ਓਟ ਤੂੰ ਸਚਾ ਸਿਰਜਨ:
The eternal Creator is proclaimed as the sole support and shelter for devotees and holy ones. The Divine Name (naam) serves as the foundation upon which the faithful lean and the refuge in which saints find protection. This direct address affirms that true security lies in the Creator's presence, not in worldly powers. The declaration functions as both praise and a reminder of where the devout must place their trust.

Themes: divine refuge, Creator's protection, naam as support, devotees' sanctuary, true shelter, saints' refuge, eternal foundation, reliance on the Divine
ਹਰਿ ਜੁਗੁ ਜੁਗੁ ਭਗਤ ਉਪਾਇਆ ਪੈਜ ਰਖਦਾ ਆਇਆ ਰਾਮ:
The Divine raises up devotees in every age and has consistently protected their dignity and honor, especially in times of crisis. This declaration affirms a historical pattern of divine faithfulness: across all eras, God creates and sustains those who devote themselves to Truth, shielding their reputation when they face trials. The statement offers reassurance that divine protection is not occasional but eternal, a continuous thread through time.

Themes: divine protection, devotees, honor preservation, historical continuity, crisis and deliverance, divine faithfulness, bhagat, divine sustenance
ਹਮਰੇ ਕਰਮ ਨ ਬਿਚਰਹੁ ਠਾਕੁਰ ਤੁਮ੍ਹ ਪੈਜ ਰਖਹੁ ਅ:
The devotee pleads with the Divine Master not to weigh their accumulated karma—virtuous and sinful deeds—but instead to preserve the honor of His own servant. This prayer of complete surrender acknowledges human unworthiness while placing full reliance on divine grace rather than merit. The Lord's prestige is bound up with protecting those who serve Him; preserving the devotee's dignity becomes a matter of divine self-interest and faithfulness to the master-servant bond.

Themes: divine grace, karma, master-servant relationship, surrender, prayer, honor, protection, humility
ਜਾਚਿਕੁ ਮੰਗੈ ਨਿਤ ਨਾਮੁ ਸਾਹਿਬੁ ਕਰੇ ਕਬੂਲੁ ॥:
The devotee positioned as a beggar who ceaselessly asks for naam (the divine Name) finds the Divine Master granting that very request. The beggar image encodes total dependence and humble petition; the promise of acceptance guarantees that unrelenting spiritual asking meets divine approval. Persistent supplication for the Name alone is never turned away — the Lord receives and fulfills what the seeker perpetually seeks.

Themes: naam, supplication, divine acceptance, persistent seeking, humility, beggar-devotee, answered prayer
ਦੇਹਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਸੰਤੋਖੀਆ ਉਤਰੈ ਮਨ ਕੀ ਭੁਖ ॥:
The seeker pleads for the gift of naam (the divine Name) as the sole remedy for inner emptiness. Receiving the Name produces santokh (contentment), which extinguishes the mind's relentless craving (trishna). Spiritual hunger and worldly thirst are quenched only through divine remembrance, not through external acquisition. The petition acknowledges that lasting satisfaction arises from the Divine presence alone, not from fulfilling desires.

Themes: naam, contentment, mind's craving, spiritual hunger, divine petition, trishna, satisfaction, surrender
ਜਾਚਿਕੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਾਚੈ ਜਾਚੈ ॥:
The speaker identifies as a beggar asking only for naam, the divine Name, from the One who is support and master of all beings. The repeated verb emphasizes unceasing, desperate seeking with no end point. This declaration of spiritual poverty positions the devotee in radical dependence and humility, modeling the posture of one who has recognized that the divine Name alone is worth begging for.

Themes: beggar, naam, spiritual poverty, surrender, persistence, humility, dependence on God, single-minded seeking
ਕਰਹੁ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਗੋਪਾਲ ਗੋਬਿਦੇ ਅਪਨਾ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਾਵਹ:
The speaker pleads with the Divine, addressed as Gopal and Gobind—names evoking the Lord as nurturer and master—to grant mercy and actively cause the remembrance of the divine Name. The causative verb form reveals that even the capacity for simran (loving remembrance) is not self-generated but bestowed through grace; devotion itself is received as gift, not achieved through effort.

Themes: divine mercy, naam simran, grace-dependent devotion, supplication, human limitation, divine names, spiritual helplessness, gift of remembrance
ਜਾਚਕੁ ਮੰਗੈ ਦਾਨੁ ਦੇਹਿ ਪਿਆਰਿਆ ॥:
The speaker positions themselves as a beggar seeking alms from the Divine, addressed intimately as Beloved. The teeka specifies that the requested gift is the infinite Word or naam (divine Name), spiritual welfare rather than material wealth. This is a prayer of utter humility and dependence, expressing complete reliance on divine generosity. The begging imagery conveys self-emptying surrender, while the tender address reveals devotion grounded in love rather than obligation.

Themes: supplication, divine gift, humility, naam, beggar imagery, beloved Lord, spiritual alms, surrender, prayer of petition
ਦਰਿ ਮੰਗਤੁ ਜਾਚੈ ਦਾਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਦੀਜੈ ਕ੍ਰਿਪਾ ਕਰਿ:
The devotee casts themselves as a beggar at the Divine threshold, pleading for the gift of grace. This is an act of complete self-lowering and supplication — the human soul acknowledging total dependence on the Lord's mercy, asking to be given what cannot be earned. The image of begging at a door conveys both destitution and trust: the seeker has nothing yet comes confidently to the Giver's entrance, expecting compassion.

Themes: divine door, begging, grace, mercy, supplication, humility, dependence, charity
ਮਉਲਿਓ ਮਨੁ ਤਨੁ ਹੋਇਓ ਹਰਿਆ ਏਕ ਬੂੰਦ ਜਿਨਿ ਪਾਈ:
The mind blooms and the body becomes verdant, spiritually alive and flourishing, when one receives even a single drop of naam, the divine Name. The image of a parched plant responding to water captures how the smallest measure of divine connection revitalizes the entire being—consciousness expanding in joy, the physical form quickened with inner vitality. The declaration affirms the extraordinary potency of sacred remembrance: a mere drop suffices to restore what had withered.

Themes: naam, transformation, mind-body, blossoming, spiritual nourishment, divine potency, grace, flourishing
ਹਰਿ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਵਤ ਸਦ ਹੀ ਰਾਤਾ ॥:
The line declares that one who drinks the divine essence, the naam-amrit (nectar of the divine Name), remains permanently saturated with that essence, forever dyed in its color. Drinking conveys internalizing the divine presence, while being dyed expresses total transformation where the devotee's entire being is permeated and permanently colored by the divine. This describes the lasting, irreversible effect of true spiritual consumption.

Themes: divine nectar, naam (divine Name), spiritual saturation, permanent transformation, internalization of the divine, color of devotion, amrit, loving remembrance
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਰਸੁ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਗਾਈਐ ਅਹਿਨਿਸਿ ਪੂਰਨ:
Instruct the mind to sing divine praises, the life-giving nectar. Continuously singing kirtan (devotional singing) causes an unbroken inner resonance of spiritual bliss to vibrate day and night. The celestial sound-current is the experiential joy of naam (the divine Name) saturating consciousness, an inner music of spiritual fulfillment replacing worldly emptiness.

Themes: kirtan, naad, inner resonance, spiritual bliss, life-giving nectar, continuous remembrance, experiential joy, divine sound-current
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਰਸਨਾ ਪੀਉ ਪਿਆਰੀ ॥:
The speaker affectionately addresses their own tongue, commanding it to drink the ambrosial nectar of the divine Name. This is self-directed instruction to engage the faculty of speech in naam simran (loving remembrance), consuming spiritual essence rather than worldly words. The amrit is the immortalizing Name-essence that gives spiritual life; the tongue must taste this nectar to fulfill its true purpose.

Themes: tongue, amrit, divine Name, self-instruction, speech discipline, spiritual nourishment, naam simran, beloved self-address
ਤੇਰਾ ਜਨੁ ਰਾਮ ਰਸਾਇਣਿ ਮਾਤਾ ॥:
The devotee lives steeped in the elixir of the divine Name, intoxicated by its essence, lost in a rapture that comes from constant absorption. Rasāyaṇ, the nectar of naam, is both the substance and the experience — the servant drinks it and is transformed by it, perpetually mast in loving remembrance. Surrender to this essence is the devotee's entire sustenance and joy.

Themes: naam, spiritual intoxication, divine elixir, devotional absorption, surrender, loving remembrance, ecstasy, servant of the Lord
ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਰਸੁ ਪੀਆ ਗੁਰ ਸਬਦੀ ਹਮ ਨਾਮ ਵਿਟਹੁ ਕ:
Through the Guru's shabad (divine word), the speaker drinks the amrit ras—the ambrosial essence, the nectar of naam (the divine Name) that grants spiritual life. This drinking is the soul's absorption of divine presence, an internal tasting of immortality. The speaker offers themselves as kurban, a sacrifice, expressing complete surrender and devotion to the Name. The shabad enables this experience of immortalizing nectar, prompting total dedication to that divine source.

Themes: naam, shabad, spiritual nourishment, surrender, Guru's grace, amrit, devotion, sacrifice
ਰਸੁ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਰਸੁ ਅਤਿ ਭਲਾ ਕਿਤੁ ਬਿਧਿ:
Declares naam (the divine Name) as the supreme ambrosial essence, the sweetest of all tastes and the giver of spiritual life, then asks how one can obtain and consume this nectar. The question is a longing — the seeker craves the experience of divine sweetness yet confesses not knowing the path to receive it. Praise of the Name's incomparable flavour intertwines with the soul's hunger for that sustaining essence.

Themes: naam as amrit (immortal nectar), longing for divine experience, seeker's question, spiritual hunger, taste of devotion, incomparable sweetness, yearning for union, path to obtaining essence
ਬਿਖੈ ਬਨੁ ਫੀਕਾ ਤਿਆਗਿ ਰੀ ਸਖੀਏ ਨਾਮੁ ਮਹਾ ਰਸੁ:
An exhortation to a spiritual companion to abandon the unsatisfying pursuit of sensory vices and instead drink deeply of the divine Name, which alone offers true sustenance. The tasteless water of worldly corruption represents maya (worldly attachment) and passions that leave the soul parched, while the supreme nectar of naam is the ever-satisfying essence. Spiritual life is framed as a decisive exchange: rejecting what is bland and empty to embrace what is flavorful and fulfilling.

Themes: naam as nectar, renunciation of vice, spiritual companionship, divine satisfaction, maya as tasteless, inner nourishment, exhortation, choice and exchange
ਕਬੀਰ ਬਿਰਹੁ ਭੁਯੰਗਮੁ ਮਨਿ ਬਸੈ ਮੰਤੁ ਨ ਮਾਨੈ ਕ:
The line declares that intense longing for the Divine, imaged as a snake coiled within the mind, cannot be cured by any mantra or ritual remedy. The snake conveys both the inescapable grip of this spiritual yearning and its capacity to consume all ordinary comfort. This state of biraha (separation) arises after taking the Guru's shelter and resists all conventional spiritual practices, marking a condition where only the Divine presence itself brings relief.

Themes: biraha, spiritual longing, snake imagery, Guru's shelter, resistance to ritual, incurable yearning, Divine separation, mind's occupation
ਹਰਿ ਬਿਨੁ ਕਿਉ ਜੀਵਾ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਈ ॥:
The speaker asks their mother a rhetorical question revealing an impossible situation: existence without the Divine is unbearable. The teeka clarifies that the soul becomes agitated and restless when separated from naam, the divine Name. This is an intimate cry of spiritual longing, expressing complete dependency on God for any meaningful life. The address to "mother" frames this distress in the most personal terms, as a confession of helplessness before one's closest confidant.

Themes: divine longing, separation from God, naam, spiritual restlessness, dependency on the Divine, viraha, soul's distress, intimate prayer
ਪ੍ਰਭ ਮਿਲਬੇ ਕਉ ਪ੍ਰੀਤਿ ਮਨਿ ਲਾਗੀ ॥:
A profound and loving yearning to unite with the Divine has taken root within the consciousness. The declaration expresses an internal spiritual awakening, marking the transformative moment when devotion becomes an anchored, deeply felt attachment to the Beloved rather than a mere practice. It announces the birth of true longing for the Creator.

Themes: divine longing, yearning for God, internal awakening, loving devotion, attachment to the Beloved, spiritual desire, preet (loving attachment), meeting the Divine
ਹਰਿ ਦਰਸਨ ਕਉ ਮੇਰਾ ਮਨੁ ਬਹੁ ਤਪਤੈ ਜਿਉ ਤ੍ਰਿਖਾ:
The mind burns with desperate longing for darshan (the blessed vision of the Divine), writhing like a parched man craving water. The teeka traces this agony to the arrow of prem (divine love) that has pierced the heart, leaving the soul restless and consumed. This is the fever of separation, the lovesick state where the mind finds no rest without beholding the Beloved, declaring that the devotee's sole sustenance is the sight of the Eternal.

Themes: darshan longing, thirst metaphor, virah (separation agony), prem as piercing arrow, mind's restless craving, lovesick devotion, yearning for divine vision, water and parched soul imagery
ਬਾਝਹੁ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਕੋਇ ਨ ਸਾਰੇ ਏਕਲੜੀ ਕੁਰਲਾਏ ॥:
The soul confesses that without the Beloved Lord, no one inquires after her welfare; she wails in utter solitude. The world-jungle offers no companionship, and the soul-bride finds herself abandoned, her cries echoing unanswered. Only the Divine Husband truly cares for this life, and in His absence, she experiences the full desolation of spiritual exile.

Themes: separation from the Divine, soul's loneliness, world as wilderness, divine as sole refuge, longing and yearning, soul-bride motif, spiritual abandonment, dependence on the Divine
ਮਨਿ ਬੈਰਾਗੁ ਭਇਆ ਦਰਸਨੁ ਦੇਖਣੈ ਕਾ ਚਾਉ ॥:
The mind has grown weary of worldly attachments and now burns with yearning for darshan, the vision of the Divine. Detachment has taken hold, displacing worldly desire with an intense thirst for the divine presence. Love for the Eternal has turned the heart away from maya (worldly attachment), producing a restless longing to behold the Beloved.

Themes: vairagya (detachment), darshan (divine vision), longing, spiritual transformation, turning away from maya, divine love, yearning, thirst for the Divine presence
ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਚਿਰੀ ਵਿਛੁੰਨਿਆ ਮਿਲੁ ਸਬਦਿ ਗੁਰੂ ਪ੍:
This passionate plea calls for reunion with the Divine after ages of separation. The devotee yearns for union through the Guru's shabad, the divine Word that bridges the separated soul and its source. A notable interpretive tension: the English reads as the soul asking to merge with God, while the teeka reads as inviting God to dwell in the devotee's heart-home.

Themes: divine union, separation and longing, Guru's shabad as bridge, heart as divine dwelling, yearning for God, reunion after ages, divine presence, surrender and invitation
ਪਿਰ ਦੋਸੁ ਨਾਹੀ ਸੁਖਹ ਦਾਤੇ ਹਉ ਵਿਛੁੜੀ ਬੁਰਿਆਰ:
The soul-bride confesses that her separation from the Divine Husband Lord stems entirely from her own wrongful actions, while the Lord remains faultless as the generous giver of peace. This admission accepts full personal responsibility for spiritual distance, exonerating the Divine and recognizing that separation is self-inflicted through evil deeds rather than caused by divine abandonment or neglect.

Themes: self-responsibility, separation from Divine, divine benevolence, confession of fault, soul-bride imagery, acceptance, human failing, spiritual distance
ਆਉ ਜੀ ਤੂ ਆਉ ਹਮਾਰੈ ਹਰਿ ਜਸੁ ਸ੍ਰਵਨ ਸੁਨਾਵਨਾ:
The devotee urgently calls out in desperate longing, repeating the plea for the divine presence to come and dwell within the heart. The teeka addresses the Guru as the one who enters and causes the ears to hear God's praise; the translation implies addressing God directly. This is complete dependence: the devotee cannot access sacred sound without that indwelling presence. The heart as home and ears as instruments of receiving point to an intimate, embodied relationship with the sacred.

Themes: divine invitation, yearning and longing, heart as dwelling place, sacred sound and hearing, dependence on the Guru, intimate presence, praise of the Divine, repeated plea
ਆਉ ਹਮਾਰੈ ਰਾਮ ਪਿਆਰੇ ਜੀਉ ॥:
The devotee pleads with the beloved Divine to come and dwell within the heart, expressing intimate yearning for divine presence and union. The soul invites Ram to take up residence inside, making the heart a home for the sacred. This is a prayer of longing that positions the inner being as a space awaiting its true inhabitant.

Themes: divine intimacy, longing for union, heart as divine dwelling, prayer of invitation, yearning, beloved Lord, divine presence, devotion
ਬਿਨਵੰਤਿ ਨਾਨਕ ਦਇਆ ਧਾਰਹੁ ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਨਾਹ ਪਿਆਰ:
The soul-bride supplicates before the Divine, addressed as the beloved Husband, begging for compassion and asking Him to come dwell within the heart. The image of the husband returning home expresses the deeper plea for divine presence to abide in the inner sanctuary of consciousness. This is a prayer of utter dependence and yearning, acknowledging that only through mercy can the separation end and union be restored.

Themes: supplication, bridal mysticism, divine indwelling, heart as sanctuary, longing for union, divine mercy, soul-bride imagery, prayer of dependence
ਮੋਹਨ ਘਰਿ ਆਵਹੁ ਕਰਉ ਜੋਦਰੀਆ ॥:
The devotee addresses the Divine as Mohan, the Enchanter who captivates hearts, and makes fervent entreaty with joined hands for Him to enter and abide in the heart-house. This intimate supplication expresses the soul's desperate longing for God to take up residence in the inner sanctuary. The house image signifies the heart as a dwelling place awaiting its eternal Guest, while the pleading stance reveals both yearning and surrender.

Themes: divine indwelling, heart as sanctuary, supplication, longing, Mohan the Enchanter, intimate prayer, surrender, divine presence within
ਹਮ ਘਰਿ ਸਾਜਨ ਆਏ ॥:
The teeka clarifies that the "friends" are the Divine Friend and the "home" is the heart. This declaration expresses the joy of spiritual awakening, where the Lord manifests within the inner sanctuary of the devotee's consciousness. It describes a state of intimate union where the Beloved resides within the self, transforming the heart into a dwelling place for the Divine presence and fulfilling the soul's deepest longing for companionship.

Themes: Divine indwelling, heart as sanctuary, spiritual awakening, intimacy with God, inner realization, Friend-Master, presence of the Beloved, joy of union.
ਪਹਿਲੈ ਪਹਰੈ ਫੁਲੜਾ ਫਲੁ ਭੀ ਪਛਾ ਰਾਤਿ ॥:
The metaphor of night watches maps the progression of spiritual practice: early devotion blooms like flowers, but the actual fruit of realization comes in the later watches, specifically amrit vela (pre-dawn hours). The teaching instructs that sustained practice through the night culminates in the early morning hours when spiritual attainment ripens. Flowers represent initial beauty; fruit represents the final goal of union with the Divine.

Themes: amrit vela, spiritual progression, night watches, flowers and fruit metaphor, meditation timing, devotional stages, early morning practice, spiritual fruition
ਕਬੀਰ ਸੂਤਾ ਕਿਆ ਕਰਹਿ ਉਠਿ ਕਿ ਨ ਜਪਹਿ ਮੁਰਾਰਿ:
An urgent admonition that uses the image of physical sleep to name the spiritual delusion of maya (worldly attachment). The speaker confronts the listener for remaining intoxicated in material entanglement, wasting the precious opportunity of human life. The call is to awaken from this slumber of attachment and immediately take up simran (loving remembrance) of the Divine. The tone carries desperate urgency, shaking the sleeper awake before life slips away unexamined.

Themes: spiritual awakening, urgency of devotion, maya as delusion, wasting human birth, simran, divine admonition, call to remembrance, spiritual slumber
ਪਰਭਾਤੇ ਪ੍ਰਭ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਿ ਗੁਰ ਕੇ ਚਰਣ ਧਿਆਇ ॥:
Rising before dawn to chant the divine Name and fix the mind on the Guru's feet is prescribed as the essential beginning of each day. The Guru's feet signify both the physical posture of surrender and the inner attitude of humility toward the one who connects the seeker to God. Naam (the divine Name) and Guru-seva (service to the Guru) are inseparable practices; remembrance flows from reverence, and both anchor the heart in devotion during the quiet hours when the mind is most receptive.

Themes: amrit vela, naam simran, Guru's feet, daily spiritual discipline, humility, surrender, loving remembrance, dawn prayer, Guru-seva, devotional meditation.
ਝਾਲਾਘੇ ਉਠਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਜਪਿ ਨਿਸਿ ਬਾਸੁਰ ਆਰਾਧਿ ॥:
The instruction urges the seeker to rise during amrit vela, the ambrosial pre-dawn hours, and chant the divine Name, then extend that remembrance through day and night. It prescribes a discipline anchored in early morning meditation but not confined to it—simran (loving remembrance) should permeate all hours. The teaching establishes both a starting point and continuous practice, urging constant Divine awareness rather than isolated prayer.

Themes: amrit vela, naam japna, continuous remembrance, daily spiritual discipline, early morning meditation, simran, devotional routine, day and night worship
ਬਾਬੀਹਾ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲੈ ਬੋਲਿਆ ਤਾਂ ਦਰਿ ਸੁਣੀ ਪ:
The rainbird's cry at dawn models the devotee who rises during amrit vela, the ambrosial pre-dawn hours, to call upon the Divine. The bird's desperate call for rain mirrors the soul's deep longing for union with the Creator. This affirmation declares that sincere early-morning prayer reaches the Divine Court and is heard by the Lord. The rainbird embodies total dependence and yearning; amrit vela represents the optimal time for spiritual practice when the mind is most receptive.

Themes: amrit vela, prayer, longing, Divine hearing, rainbird metaphor, dawn meditation, Divine Court, yearning
ਛਾਤੀ ਸੀਤਲ ਮਨੁ ਸੁਖੀ ਛੰਤ ਗੋਬਿਦ ਗੁਨ ਗਾਇ ॥:
The heart becomes cool and the mind finds peace through singing the virtues of Govind, the Lord of the Universe. The cooling image describes relief from the burning heat of worldly desire and anxiety, while the peaceful mind indicates the fruit of devotional practice. Singing divine qualities transforms inner turmoil into tranquility, settling the restless heart through loving engagement with the sacred Name.

Themes: devotional singing, inner peace, cooling of the heart, divine virtues, transformation of consciousness, relief from suffering, Govind, sukh
ਜੋਗੁ ਬਨਿਆ ਤੇਰਾ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਗਾਈ ॥੧॥:
The speaker declares that singing the Divine's praises constitutes true yoga—the spiritual union that yogis seek through austere practices. Through kirtan (devotional singing of God's glories), one attains both worldly contentment and ascetic fulfillment simultaneously. The act of praising the Divine becomes itself the path of union, replacing external yogic discipline with loving devotion as the genuine means of spiritual accomplishment.

Themes: yoga as devotion, kirtan as spiritual practice, union through praise, true discipline, devotion over renunciation, singing as spiritual path, divine connection through song, inner fulfillment
ਹਉ ਅਨਦਿਨੁ ਹਰਿ ਨਾਮੁ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਕਰਉ ॥:
The speaker declares an unwavering personal commitment to sing the divine Name and praise the Divine continuously, day and night, without pause. This affirmation dedicates every moment to kirtan, the devotional singing of God's virtues, and to naam, the sacred Name that anchors the heart in constant remembrance. The statement expresses resolve, devotion, and the complete orientation of life toward the Divine through unceasing worship and spiritual practice.

Themes: continuous devotion, naam (divine Name), kirtan (singing praises), day and night remembrance, personal commitment, unceasing worship, divine praise, spiritual discipline
ਰੁਣ ਝੁਣੋ ਸਬਦੁ ਅਨਾਹਦੁ ਨਿਤ ਉਠਿ ਗਾਈਐ ਸੰਤਨ ਕ:
The instruction prescribes the daily discipline of rising early to join the sangat (company of the devout) and sing God's praise in sweet, continuous melody. This kirtan (devotional singing) attunes the practitioner to the anahad shabad, the unstruck celestial sound that resonates eternally within as the primal vibration. The outer practice of chanting divine qualities in holy company opens access to the inner divine Word, connecting individual consciousness to the eternal sound current.

Themes: early rising, sangat (holy company), anahad shabad (unstruck celestial sound), kirtan (devotional singing), divine praise, spiritual discipline, attunement, sound current
ਸਾਧੋ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਕੇ ਗੁਨ ਗਾਵਉ ॥:
An exhortation calling upon holy seekers and saints to continuously sing the virtues of Gobind, the Divine Lord who sustains the world. The instruction demands ongoing, uninterrupted devotion through sacred song and praise, not occasional practice. This call to the spiritual community emphasizes kirtan (singing divine praises) as the path of constant remembrance, where vocalizing divine qualities becomes the means of staying connected to the Eternal.

Themes: kirtan, continuous devotion, divine virtues, Gobind, spiritual community, remembrance through song, praise, constant practice
ਨਿਰਬਾਣ ਕੀਰਤਨੁ ਗਾਵਹੁ ਕਰਤੇ ਕਾ ਨਿਮਖ ਸਿਮਰਤ ਜ:
An urgent instruction to sing the Creator's praise through kirtan (devotional singing) from a state emptied of craving, for even one instant of simran (loving remembrance) then liberates from all vice. Nirbaan—freedom from vasna (worldly desire)—enables true praise, whose grace makes momentary divine focus sufficient for complete release from vikaar (moral corruption).

Themes: kirtan, simran, liberation from vice, freedom from desire, the Creator, momentary remembrance, nirbaan, divine praise
ਮਨ ਮੀਠ ਤੁਹਾਰੋ ਕੀਓ ॥੧॥ ਰਹਾਉ ॥:
The speaker declares that whatever the Divine does is sweet to the mind, expressing complete acceptance of God's will without resistance. The teeka adds that the speaker has never placed blame on anyone for any wrong suffered, indicating a state where all events are received as the Divine's doing rather than attributed to human agents. This is surrender to bhana (Divine will), finding contentment rather than bitterness in every circumstance.

Themes: Divine will, acceptance, surrender, bhana, contentment, sweetness, non-blame, equanimity, trust
ਮੀਤ ਕੇ ਕਰਤਬ ਕੁਸਲ ਸਮਾਨਾ ॥੧॥:
The speaker declares that the actions of the Divine Friend are pleasing and agreeable, experienced as sources of comfort and joy rather than resistance. This expresses complete acceptance of God's will, a state where the devotee finds satisfaction in whatever the Beloved does, harmonizing personal preference with divine orchestration. The relationship is one of intimate friendship where divine deeds bring sukha (spiritual ease) and are received without complaint or condition.

Themes: divine friendship, acceptance of God's will, contentment, surrender, spiritual ease, divine actions, sukha, harmonizing with the Beloved, trust in the Friend
ਸਰਬ ਸੁਖ ਆਨੰਦ ਮੰਗਲ ਰਸ ਮਾਨਿ ਗੋਬਿੰਦੈ ਆਗਿਓ ॥:
The speaker declares that accepting God's will as sweet brings complete peace, bliss, and auspiciousness. Total fulfillment—every comfort, joy, wellbeing, and spiritual delight—arrives through embracing divine governance. This is not passive resignation but a willing, loving acceptance of hukam (divine order) that transforms all experience into contentment and sweetness.

Themes: acceptance of divine will, surrender and contentment, spiritual fulfillment, hukam (divine order), bliss through submission, peace through acceptance, divine grace, transformation of experience
ਖਿਨ ਮਹਿ ਥਾਪਿ ਉਥਾਪਨਹਾਰਾ ਆਪਨ ਹਾਥਿ ਮਤਾਤ ॥੧॥:
The Divine wields absolute power to establish and dissolve all existence within a single moment, creating and destroying at will. The image of matters held in divine hands signifies that every judgment, decree, and outcome rests solely with the Creator, who alone controls the rise and fall of creation. This declaration affirms supreme sovereignty and effortless command over cosmic and worldly affairs.

Themes: divine sovereignty, creation and dissolution, omnipotence, divine will, cosmic control, supreme authority, transient existence, divine power
ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮੁ ਧਿਆਈਐ ਕਾਰਜੁ ਆਵੈ ਰਾਸਿ ॥੧॥:
The line instructs that one should keep the remembrance of the Divine constantly dwelling within the mind, and promises that every task and affair will thereby be brought to successful completion. It establishes a cause-and-effect relationship between internal spiritual practice and external accomplishment: naam simran, the loving remembrance of the divine Name, is the means by which all endeavors reach their intended end. The teaching offers both direction and assurance.

Themes: naam simran, divine remembrance, accomplishment of tasks, spiritual practice and worldly success, meditation, divine grace, fulfillment, resolution of affairs
ਕਾਰਜੁ ਤੇਰਾ ਹੋਵੈ ਪੂਰਾ ਹਰਿ ਹਰਿ ਹਰਿ ਗੁਣ ਗਾਇ:
The line instructs the self to sing God's virtues and promises that through this devotion, all tasks and purposes reach completion. It addresses the mind directly, urging constant remembrance of the Divine Name as the means by which life's affairs are fulfilled and brought to fruition. The repetition of "Har" emphasizes the potency of divine invocation. This is both instruction and assurance: the devotee who sings God's glories finds their endeavors successfully concluded.

Themes: divine name, self-exhortation, fulfillment of purpose, devotion and worldly success, mind instruction, singing praises, Har, assurance of grace, naam simran
ਨਾਨਕ ਨਾਮੁ ਅਰਾਧਣਾ ਕਾਰਜੁ ਆਵੈ ਰਾਸਿ ॥੮॥:
The instruction declares that worshipping the Divine Name accomplishes all objectives and brings every endeavor to its proper completion. Through the power of naam simran (loving remembrance), life's core purpose reaches fulfillment and all affairs find their resolution. The statement affirms that spiritual practice centered on the Name is the means by which human life succeeds, worldly concerns are settled, and the soul's journey bears fruit.

Themes: naam simran, fulfillment of life purpose, resolution of affairs, efficacy of devotion, spiritual accomplishment, success through the Name, life objectives fulfilled
ਸਭੇ ਕਾਜ ਸਵਾਰਿਐ ਜਾ ਤੁਧੁ ਭਾਵੰਦਾ ॥੭॥:
All affairs are set right when the Divine is pleased, when divine will operates. The statement establishes a principle: matters resolve not through personal striving but through alignment with God's pleasure and acceptance. This declares both the condition for resolution—living in accordance with what pleases the Divine—and the result: harmony in all concerns, worldly and spiritual.

Themes: divine will, divine pleasure, resolution of affairs, surrender, grace, alignment with God's purpose, harmony, dependence on divine favor
ਸਗਲ ਮਨੋਰਥ ਪੂਰਨ ਹੋਏ ਕਦੇ ਨ ਹੋਇ ਦੁਖਾਲਾ ਜੀਉ:
The speaker declares that through connection with the Divine, all desires and aspirations of the heart are completely fulfilled, and suffering ends permanently. This describes the state of spiritual completion where one who has attained the Divine presence experiences lasting contentment, never again falling into sorrow. The proclamation affirms that true satisfaction comes only through divine union, which ends the cycle of unfulfilled wants and grief forever.

Themes: fulfillment of desires, end of suffering, spiritual completion, divine union, permanent peace, liberation from grief, heart's contentment, state of satisfaction
